title: In 158 TESS complex periodic variables, large flares change the dip pattern more often than chance only when corotation is within about 4 stellar radii; detected flares explain 4-11% of dip collapses
abstract: Complex periodic variables (CPVs) are young M dwarfs with sharp dips at the rotation period, probably from magnetically held material near corotation. An earlier study stated that sudden dip collapses are almost always linked with flares, from about five events in two stars. We tested this in all TESS 2-minute sectors (2018-2026) of 158 CPVs: 620 sectors, 32,479 rotation cycles and 2,733 impulsive flares. A two-sided flare detector does not mistake step changes of the dips for flares. For each flare cycle, we compared the folded pattern of the 3 cycles after with the 3 cycles before, and ranked the change among flare-free cycles of the same sector that carry the same flare mask. For flares with equivalent duration >= 300 s (about 1e34 erg), 33.7% (95% interval 26.4-41.5%) of changes are above the 90th percentile of controls, against 12.9% expected; for 100-300 s, 19.5%; below 100 s, no significant effect. The effect stays when we skip one more cycle on each side or triple the flare masks, so it is not flare light. Sharp dips fill and deepen at similar rates, so flares rearrange the material. Injections show that the largest-flare excess equals a complete removal of one dip after 35-53% of these flares. The response depends on the corotation-to-stellar radius ratio x: it is strong at x < 4.2 and absent at x > 4.2 (slope against log10 x -0.37, interval -0.60 to -0.15), with equal injection sensitivity. Of 1,041 abrupt dip collapses, 24.1% have a flare within one cycle against 17.0% by chance, so flares explain 7% (4-11%), at most about 21% with hidden flares. Thus flares disturb the corotating material only when it is close to the star, and they are not the main cause of dip evolution. Limitations: association, not proven cause; long windows at long periods can dilute short changes; approximate x and energies; one band. Code, derived tables and hashes are included; TESS files are not.
